title: The Dice Foundry
pitch: A night-shift foundry where the visitor melts a heap of rubble dice into new ones: every face on two dice is editable, and the exact sum odds redraw as a cascade of bars while a worker rolls ten million times to prove it. Puzzle orders ask for impossible-sounding things, such as two dice that are not the usual pair yet give exactly the usual sum odds, or three dice that beat each other in a loop. The visitor loses the argument that only the ordinary dice can do it, then ships the winning pair as a shareable link.
whyNow: Timeless: the dice maths never ages, and a tactile workbench with real puzzles fills the interest slot without repeating a coin-pattern race or a shuffle study.

research.summary: Two six-sided dice can be relabelled so the sum odds match ordinary dice exactly; with positive whole-number faces there is exactly one such non-standard pair (1-2-2-3-3-4 and 1-3-4-5-6-8). The reason is a polynomial factorisation that the page can show as coloured factor tiles, which turns a trick into a mechanic. A second classic, a four-dice cycle where each die beats the next with probability 2/3, gives a contrast puzzle. The scout also checked both results by brute force on 2026-10-10: only two positive relabelings exist with faces up to 11, and the four-dice cycle has exactly the stated 2/3 edges (one non-adjacent pair is 4/9). The page can verify all of this exactly in the browser, and a worker simulation shows sampling noise shrinking.

sources.title: Sicherman dice
sources.snippet: Describes the pair 1-2-2-3-3-4 and 1-3-4-5-6-8 that matches the sum odds of two normal dice, and says it is the only such non-standard pair with positive integer faces.

sources.title: Sicherman Dice
sources.snippet: Explains the generating-function factorisation that shows the relabeling exists and that no other positive-integer relabeling works.

sources.title: Abnormal normal dice
sources.snippet: A popular write-up of the same pair, noting that other matching relabelings need zeros or negative numbers.

sources.title: Revisiting Dice Relabeling Using Cyclotomic Polynomials
sources.snippet: Research note that re-derives dice relabeling through factoring over cyclotomic polynomials.
sources.note: Second independent source for the factorisation method

sources.title: On cyclic and nontransitive probabilities
sources.snippet: Paper covering cycles of dice where each beats the next; the standard four-dice set has each beating its neighbour with probability 2/3.

sources.title: Efronsche Wuerfel (educational PDF)
sources.snippet: Science-centre handout describing the four non-transitive dice and their 2/3 win chances in a loop.

sources.title: Daily Illuminator, May 2026
sources.snippet: A short piece mentioning the dice pair and giving 1977 as the year they were found; other results say 1978.
sources.note: Only evidence of the invention-year disagreement

facts.claim: As of 2026-10-10, two six-sided dice faced 1-2-2-3-3-4 and 1-3-4-5-6-8 give the same sum odds as two ordinary dice, and among positive whole-number faces this is the only non-standard pair.

The relabeling can be derived by factoring the sum-odds polynomial of one die over cyclotomic polynomials and redistributing the factors; the same factoring shows no other positive-integer pair works.
In the standard four-dice cycle (A 0,0,4,4,4,4; B 1,1,1,5,5,5; C 2,2,2,2,6,6; D 3 on every face) B beats A, C beats B, D beats C and A beats D, each with probability 2/3.

Scout's own exhaustive check on 2026-10-10 (faces 1 to 11, two dice, matching the ordinary 36-outcome sum table) found exactly two solutions: the ordinary pair and the Sicherman pair; also in that set A beats C with probability 4/9.
Sources disagree on the year the pair was found (1977 versus 1978), so the page says only 'late 1970s' or omits the year.

design.coreLoop: The visitor receives a work order, edits faces on one to four dice, watches exact sum or win-matrix charts update live, and presses the foundry button to test the order against a ten-million-roll simulation. Orders escalate from easy (make sevens likeliest) to surprising (match ordinary sums with different faces, close a three-way beating loop, make a pair that ties more often than an ordinary pair), and a free-play mode keeps rewarding tinkering because the factor tiles and win matrix reveal why a change works.
sophisticationHooks: Exact odds via convolution and polynomial factor tiles, so the page explains why a relabeling works instead of only asserting it
A worker rolls ten million seeded rolls and a cascade chart shows simulation noise converging on the exact bars
A win-matrix for up to four dice that highlights loops and ties, with an order set of about twelve bundled puzzles and hints
Shareable URL hash that encodes the dice faces so a solved order can be sent as a link
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: face editor for up to four dice (4 to 12 sides), exact distribution and win-matrix engine, factor-tile view for two dice, worker simulation with a cascade chart, about twelve hand-written work orders with a checker, hash state, light and dark, reduced motion, about panel. Cut: loaded-die weights beyond a simple weight slider, accounts, scores, sound.
risks: Nearby ground: another candidate covers a coin-pattern race with a second-mover edge; the cycle puzzles here must stay a minor part and the lead puzzle must be the sum-odds relabeling.
The invention year of the relabeling is unverified; show 'late 1970s' or leave it out.
The claim that no loading of two dice can make all sums equally likely was not sourced by the scout; leave it out unless a source is found.
Factor-tile view is the hardest piece; fall back to exact bars only if time runs short.
